variants.title: Earn authority boundary by boundary
variants.context: A request earns authority one boundary at a time: the client supplies untrusted values; the edge enforces TLS, size and rate limits, and safe parsing; the application validates the session and authorizes the action against the loaded resource, tenant, and state; interpreters receive bound parameters and context-encoded output; effects happen only with independent evidence.
variants.prompt: A request to delete an invoice arrives. Put the boundaries in order.

items.text: The client supplies route parameters, body, headers, cookies, and origin context: all untrusted.
The edge enforces TLS, request-size and rate limits, and safe parsing.
The application validates the session, then authorizes delete against the loaded invoice, tenant, relationship, and current state.
Parameters are bound for the database; any rendered values are encoded for their output context.
The delete happens only with independent evidence for identity, authority, input meaning, and intent.

variants.hint: A later service must not infer authority because middleware accepted the request.
variants.explanation: Client → edge → authorize the operation → constrain interpretation → effect.

variants.title: Earn authority boundary by boundary
variants.context: A request earns authority one boundary at a time: the client supplies untrusted values; the edge enforces TLS, size and rate limits, and safe parsing; the application validates the session and authorizes the action against the loaded resource, tenant, and state; interpreters receive bound parameters and context-encoded output; effects happen only with independent evidence.
variants.prompt: A user with a valid session requests another tenant’s report. Put the boundaries in order, showing where it stops.

items.text: Untrusted input names a report ID.
The edge admits a well-formed request.
Authorization loads the report and finds the tenant does not match: rejected here.
Interpreter binding never runs.
No effect occurs.

variants.hint: A valid session is only one input to authorization.
variants.explanation: Object-level checks happen with the resource and business state at the point of use.

variants.title: Earn authority boundary by boundary
variants.context: A request earns authority one boundary at a time: the client supplies untrusted values; the edge enforces TLS, size and rate limits, and safe parsing; the application validates the session and authorizes the action against the loaded resource, tenant, and state; interpreters receive bound parameters and context-encoded output; effects happen only with independent evidence.
variants.prompt: A search field contains a SQL fragment. Put the boundaries in order.

items.text: The client supplies the string.
The edge bounds size and parses safely.
Authorization confirms the caller may search this tenant.
The query binds the string as a parameter, so it stays data.
Results are returned; no injected SQL executed.

variants.hint: Validation alone does not make string-built code safe.
variants.explanation: Parameter binding is the interpreter-specific control.

variants.title: Separate the questions
variants.context: Authenticate the principal, authorize the operation against the object and tenant, and constrain interpretation with parameter binding and contextual encoding. A protected route is not a protected operation.
variants.prompt: A route guard checks that the user is logged in, then any logged-in user can edit any order. Which control is missing?
options: Object-level authorization against the loaded order, tenant, and state.
optionFeedback: Authentication identifies; it does not grant authority over every record.
Passwords are unrelated to authorization.
Validation is about meaning, not permission.
variants.hint: Who may touch this specific object?
variants.explanation: A protected route is not a protected operation.

variants.title: Separate the questions
variants.context: Authenticate the principal, authorize the operation against the object and tenant, and constrain interpretation with parameter binding and contextual encoding. A protected route is not a protected operation.
variants.prompt: A query is built by concatenating a validated string. Is it safe?
options: No. Use parameter binding; validation does not make string-built code safe.
Yes, if the string is short.
optionFeedback: Binding keeps data from becoming syntax.
Validation constrains meaning, not interpretation.
Length is irrelevant.
variants.explanation: Match the defense to the interpreter.

variants.title: Separate the questions
variants.context: Authenticate the principal, authorize the operation against the object and tenant, and constrain interpretation with parameter binding and contextual encoding. A protected route is not a protected operation.
variants.prompt: A JWT’s algorithm and key are chosen from the token itself. Which question was answered wrongly?
options: Authentication: do not accept algorithms, keys, or identity claims chosen by untrusted input.
optionFeedback: The verifier chooses trusted keys and algorithms.
Authorization comes after authentication.
Interpretation concerns interpreters, not identity.
variants.hint: Which control decides who the principal is?
variants.explanation: Validate issuer, audience, expiry, revocation, and strength from configuration.

variants.title: Compose browser controls
variants.context: CSP with nonces constrains script execution; CORS controls browser reads, not authorization; frame-ancestors must be a response header; SameSite is site-based and weaker than same-origin policy.
variants.prompt: A CSP is set in a meta tag with frame-ancestors, but the page can still be framed. Why?
options: frame-ancestors is not supported in a CSP meta element; send it as an HTTP response header.
optionFeedback: frame-ancestors also does not inherit from default-src.
Nonces concern scripts.
Meta CSP works for some directives, not this one.
variants.hint: Which delivery mechanism does this directive require?
variants.explanation: Set frame-ancestors in the HTTP response.

variants.title: Compose browser controls
variants.context: CSP with nonces constrains script execution; CORS controls browser reads, not authorization; frame-ancestors must be a response header; SameSite is site-based and weaker than same-origin policy.
variants.prompt: A preflight succeeds for a partner origin. Does that authorize the request?
options: No. CORS controls browser access to a response; it is not authentication or authorization.
optionFeedback: The endpoint still needs its own authorization.
CORS is a browser policy.
Credentials mode does not grant authority.
variants.explanation: Never treat a successful preflight as resource authorization.

variants.title: Compose browser controls
variants.context: CSP with nonces constrains script execution; CORS controls browser reads, not authorization; frame-ancestors must be a response header; SameSite is site-based and weaker than same-origin policy.
variants.prompt: A cookie uses SameSite=Strict, so the team removes CSRF tokens. What is the gap?
options: SameSite is site-based, not origin-based; sibling subdomains can be same-site. Keep an independent intent check.
optionFeedback: Treat SameSite as defense in depth.
The boundary differs from same-origin policy.
Strict has usability costs but that is not the security gap.
variants.hint: How does a site differ from an origin?
variants.explanation: CSRF tokens, Origin checks, or Fetch Metadata provide independent intent evidence.

variants.title: Match the defense
variants.context: Input sanitization is not universal. Preserve the value as data, then apply the interpreter-specific control: parameter binding for queries, contextual encoding for HTML, a real URL parser and network restrictions for outbound requests, server-side names and content verification for uploads.
variants.prompt: A function strips angle brackets from every input on the way in. Is the app safe from injection?
options: No. Sanitization is not universal; encode for each output context and bind parameters for each interpreter.
optionFeedback: URL, attribute, CSS, JavaScript, and SQL contexts need different handling.
One transformation cannot fit every interpreter.
Even HTML needs context-specific encoding.
variants.hint: Which interpreter will consume this value?
variants.explanation: Preserve the value as data and apply the correct control at the consumer.

variants.title: Match the defense
variants.context: Input sanitization is not universal. Preserve the value as data, then apply the interpreter-specific control: parameter binding for queries, contextual encoding for HTML, a real URL parser and network restrictions for outbound requests, server-side names and content verification for uploads.
variants.prompt: A feature fetches a user-supplied URL server-side. Which controls reduce SSRF?
options: Parse with a real URL parser, resolve and constrain destinations, block private and metadata networks, and recheck redirects.
optionFeedback: Destination control is the SSRF defense.
Scheme alone does not stop internal targets.
Size limits do not stop internal reads.
variants.hint: Where could this request end up?
variants.explanation: Outbound URLs are an interpreter of their own.

variants.title: Match the defense
variants.context: Input sanitization is not universal. Preserve the value as data, then apply the interpreter-specific control: parameter binding for queries, contextual encoding for HTML, a real URL parser and network restrictions for outbound requests, server-side names and content verification for uploads.
variants.prompt: Users upload files that are served back from the main origin. Which controls apply?
options: Generate server-side names, verify type by content, scan when required, and serve active content from an isolated origin.
Serve from the same origin for simplicity.
optionFeedback: Uploads become code when served from a privileged origin.
Extensions are attacker-controlled.
Same-origin serving lets uploads run with the site’s authority.
variants.hint: What can an uploaded file do on your origin?

variants.title: Design the lifecycle
variants.context: Authentication is a lifecycle: establish identity, issue bounded sessions, recheck sensitive actions, revoke and investigate.
variants.prompt: A new account system is designed. Put the lifecycle in order.

items.text: Verify ownership of the chosen factor and protect registration and recovery from enumeration.
Issue short-lived, purpose-bound sessions with memory-hard password hashing and MFA where warranted.
Require fresh authentication or explicit confirmation for high-consequence operations.
Rotate identifiers after privilege changes, revoke on compromise, preserve minimized evidence, and notify users.

variants.title: Design the lifecycle
variants.context: Authentication is a lifecycle: establish identity, issue bounded sessions, recheck sensitive actions, revoke and investigate.
variants.prompt: A user’s session is suspected compromised. Put the response in order, within the lifecycle.

items.text: Their identity was established at enrollment.
Their session was issued with a bounded lifetime.
Sensitive actions were rechecked with fresh authentication.
Revoke sessions, rotate identifiers, preserve evidence, notify, and verify recovery from a clean state.

variants.hint: Recovery is the last stage, and it must be designed, not improvised.

variants.title: Design the lifecycle
variants.context: Authentication is a lifecycle: establish identity, issue bounded sessions, recheck sensitive actions, revoke and investigate.
variants.prompt: Password reset is being hardened. Put the lifecycle stages it touches in order.

items.text: Protect recovery from enumeration and abuse with rate limits and consistent public responses.
Issue a bounded session after verified recovery.
Recheck sensitive actions after the reset.
Rotate identifiers and record the event for investigation.

variants.explanation: Rate-limit login, MFA, reset, and recovery by multiple signals.
